Pre-instruction drawings: self-portrait,:
Edwards opens her course with these three and they are not a warm-up. They are the control group. Draw them before reading anything else, date them, and put them somewhere you will not be tempted to improve them.

Self-portrait from a mirror, your own non-drawing hand, and a chair. Half an hour each at most. They will be bad in specific ways — the eyes halfway up a too-short head, the hand a symbol with five sausages, the chair drawn from what you know a chair is rather than from the angles actually in front of you.

That badness is the data. Stage 8 redraws all three, and the comparison is the only honest measure of a year's work that does not depend on how you feel about it on the day.
Upside-down drawing: copy a line drawing:
Take a line drawing — Edwards uses Picasso's Stravinsky — turn it upside down, and copy it without ever turning it the right way up.

It works because inverted the image stops being nameable. You cannot draw the symbol for a hand if you cannot tell it is a hand, so you are forced to copy the angle and length actually there. Almost everyone's inverted copy is dramatically better than their right-way-up one, and finding that out about yourself is the point of the exercise.

Do not peek. The moment you recognise what you are drawing, the symbol system switches back on and you will watch your own accuracy fall.
20 blind contour drawings of your own ha:
Eyes on the hand, never on the paper. Pen, so you cannot erase. Move the pen only as fast as your eye travels along the edge — slowly.

The results are grotesque and that is expected. Blind contour is not for producing a drawing, it is for coupling eye to hand: it trains you to look at the model far more than at the page, which is the single habit that separates people who draw accurately from people who do not.

Twenty, because the first five are self-conscious. Your own hand because it is free, always available, and one of the hardest things in the body.
20 modified contour drawings of everyday:
The same discipline with permission to glance. Look at the paper only when you need to reposition the pen, never while drawing a line.

This is the usable version of blind contour — it keeps the slow edge-following and recovers enough control that the drawing holds together. Everything after this stage is drawn this way whether or not it is called contour.

Objects with awkward edges rather than simple ones: a crumpled sock, keys, a pair of scissors, a plug and its cable. Smooth round things let you fall back on the symbol.
10 negative-space drawings — draw the ga:
Draw a chair by drawing only the holes in it. The spaces between the rungs, between the legs, between the chair and the frame of your paper. Do not draw the chair.

Negative space has no name, so there is no symbol to substitute. When the gaps are right the object appears, correctly, without you ever having drawn it — which is a convincing demonstration that your eye was always capable and your symbol system was in the way.

Use things with lots of gaps: a bicycle, a stepladder, a stack of chairs, a houseplant. Close the composition by treating the paper edge as part of the shape.
Sighting: angles and proportions measure:
The pencil-at-arm's-length business, done properly. Lock your elbow, close one eye, and hold the pencil so it stays in the same plane every time — if your arm bends the measurements are meaningless.

Two separate skills. ANGLE: hold the pencil along an edge and read it as a clock angle against true vertical or horizontal, then transfer it. PROPORTION: pick one unit — the head, the hand, the width of the jaw — and measure everything else in that unit.

This is the technique that makes observational accuracy a procedure rather than a talent. It feels mechanical for about a month and then becomes invisible.
Draw one object five times across a week:
One object, five sittings, no comparison until the fifth is finished. Then lay them out in order.

What this teaches is not about the object. It is that drawing the same thing again is not repetition — each attempt starts from a different understanding, and you can watch the understanding change. It also breaks the habit of treating a drawing as a one-shot performance to be got right.

Pick something with enough structure to stay interesting: a shoe, a skull if you have one, a hand mixer, a bicycle saddle.
Keys to Drawing: work the exercises in t:
Dodson is the practical complement to Edwards. Where she argues about the two hemispheres, he just gives you the procedures and the reasons.

The first third covers restating lines rather than erasing, drawing what you see at the edges of vision, and the single most useful idea in the book: that the drawing problems people call talent are almost all problems of attention. Work the exercises as written rather than reading past them.

This closes stage 1. If the upside-down drawing and the negative space exercises landed, the Dodson exercises will feel like confirmation rather than instruction, which is how you know you are ready to move on.
100 thirty-second gestures (Vilppu, Draw:
Thirty seconds, a hundred times. Use Line of Action with the timer set, or any reference that changes on its own so you cannot linger.

Thirty seconds is short enough that detail is impossible, which is the design. You get one idea per drawing: where the weight is, which way the spine curves, what the figure is DOING. Vilppu's whole argument is that this is the drawing and everything after is decoration on it.

Do not tidy them. Do not go back. A hundred bad fast drawings teach more than ten careful ones, and the first thirty of these will be bad in a way that is simply the cost of entry.
100 more, from life if there is any life:
The same again, and the number is not padding — the second hundred is where the hand stops panicking and starts choosing.

From life if you can get it: a life-drawing session, people in a café, anyone sitting still for a minute. Life is better than reference because a photograph has already flattened the form and made the decision about where the light is. A living model moves slightly, and drawing something that moves forces you to draw the idea rather than the outline.

If there is no life available, this is not an excuse to skip it. Reference is worth 80% of it and 80% of two hundred gestures is still two hundred gestures.
Line of action identified and drawn firs:
One line, before anything else, every time. From the pit of the neck through the spine to the weight-bearing foot, as a single curve.

Fifty figures where that line goes down first and the rest is built on it. The test of whether you have it is that the line should be drawable in under a second and should still read as the pose with nothing else on the page.

The common failure is drawing the line of action as the actual spine. It is not anatomy, it is the direction of the energy — it often runs outside the body entirely on a figure leaning hard.
Contour and gesture combined — the first:
Nicolaides pairs them deliberately: contour trains the eye to follow an edge slowly, gesture trains the hand to state a whole thing fast, and he thinks neither works without the other.

His instruction is to do both every day rather than one then the other. A contour drawing then a gesture of the same model, alternating, within one session.

What you are looking for is a drawing that has the speed of a gesture and the specificity of a contour. It will not happen for a while. It is still the thing being aimed at for the rest of the curriculum.
Nicolaides' first month of the schedule,:
The Natural Way to Draw contains an actual timetable — hours per day, which exercise, in which order, for a year. Do the first month of it as written.

It is demanding and it is from 1941 and it is still the most complete drawing course anyone has written down. The schedule matters more than any individual exercise in it: the point is daily contact with the same problems, not variety.

If the full daily hours are not possible, scale the whole schedule down proportionally rather than dropping exercises. Dropping the ones that feel unproductive removes exactly the ones doing the work.
50 one-minute gestures with weight — whe:
A minute is four times thirty seconds and the extra three are for one question: where is the weight?

Find the weight-bearing foot, mark the ground, and get the pelvis tilted the way a body actually tilts when it stands on one leg — hip up on the supporting side, shoulders tipping the other way. A figure drawn without this floats, no matter how good the limbs are.

Fifty. Mark the ground line on every one, even when the reference is cropped. A figure with no floor is the single most common failure in game art and you are about to be drawing a lot of it.
20 one-minute animal gestures (Vilppu, D:
Animals, because the same principles have to survive a different skeleton — and because Shepherds has sheep, a fox, a dog and a deer in it before it has anything else.

Vilppu's approach is unchanged from the human: line of action first, then the two masses (ribcage and pelvis) and how they connect. A quadruped is the same two boxes rotated and strung along a longer spine.

Twenty, mixed: something with a long spine, something stocky, something with a lot of fur hiding the form. The fur one is the most useful, because it forces you to draw the animal under it.
50 spheres, 50 boxes, 50 cylinders — fro:
A hundred and fifty forms, freehand, no reference, no ruler, no ellipse guide.

The boxes are the hard ones. A box drawn from imagination is a test of whether you understand perspective yet, and most of the first fifty will have edges that imply three contradictory vanishing points. Draw them anyway; the fifty is what teaches it, not the explanation.

Vary the angle on every one. Fifty boxes seen from the same three-quarter view is one box drawn fifty times, which teaches nothing. Above the horizon, below it, tilted, foreshortened hard.
Cross-contour lines on a sphere, a cylin:
Lines that run ACROSS the form rather than around its outline — the way a net stretched over an object would sit.

It is the fastest way to find out whether you are drawing a shape or a volume. Cross-contours on a sphere are easy and prove nothing. On a folded cloth they are brutal, because every fold turns the surface and the lines have to turn with it.

Do the cloth last, and do it from life with an actual towel thrown over a chair. Cloth is in nearly every drawing you will ever make and it is the thing most people never practise.
The same forms with one light source and:
One source, stated and consistent. The three primitives again, now with: a lit plane, the terminator where the form turns away, the core shadow sitting ON the terminator, reflected light inside the shadow, and the cast shadow on the ground.

The mistake to watch for is making the core shadow lighter than the cast shadow. It is darker — the cast shadow catches bounce light from everywhere, the core shadow catches almost none. Getting that one relationship right is most of what makes a drawn form look solid.

This is also the exact light logic the Shepherds art contract bakes in at upper-left, so what you learn here transfers directly.
50 mannequin figures from imagination (L:
Loomis' simplified figure: ribcage as a modified box, pelvis as a smaller box, limbs as tapered cylinders, joints as spheres. No anatomy, no detail, no face.

Fifty from imagination means fifty without reference. You will run out of poses around fifteen and that is when it starts working, because inventing a pose forces you to understand the structure rather than copy it.

Loomis' proportion system — eight heads for a heroic figure, seven and a half for a realistic one — goes in here and then gets used for the rest of your life. Learn where the halfway point of the body is. It is not the waist.
Block in a figure from reference, 20 tim:
The full sequence on one drawing, twenty times: line of action, then the two masses, then the limbs as cylinders, then the contour over the top.

Gesture FIRST is the rule being enforced here. The temptation after fifty mannequins is to start with the boxes, and a figure built box-first comes out stiff every time. Thirty seconds of gesture, then build on it.

Twenty is enough because this is integration rather than new material. If it is still fighting you at twenty, the gesture work is the part to go back to, not the construction.
Vilppu: sphere, box and cylinder applied:
Vilppu's distinctive move: he does not draw the forms as separate objects, he finds them inside a living figure while drawing it. The ribcage IS a box and he draws it as one, in the middle of a flowing contour.

The skill is switching between the two ways of seeing without stopping — gesture line, then suddenly a box for the pelvis, then back to contour. He demonstrates it constantly in the Drawing Manual and it is the thing worth stealing from him.

From life if you can. The whole point is that it is happening to a figure that is breathing rather than to a diagram.
The figure in eight directions, standing:
The same figure, same pose, rotated: e, ne, n, nw, w, sw, s, se. By hand, from imagination, on one sheet.

This is Timon's actual problem drawn out. The approved body bases are eight-direction, and until you can rotate a figure in your head you cannot judge whether a set of eight is consistent — which is the thing the art contract most needs a second pair of eyes on.

The back three-quarters are the hard ones and the ones people fudge. Check them against each other: the shoulder width, the head size and the stride must not change between directions, and any that do will read as a wobble when the sprite turns.
Foreshortening: 20 limbs pointing at the:
An arm pointing straight at you is a circle with a hand on it, and every instinct you have will want to lengthen it.

Twenty, from reference, deliberately extreme. The technique is cross-contour: draw the overlapping cylinder sections as rings, let them stack, and trust the overlaps to say what the length cannot. Overlap is what reads as depth; foreshortened length is almost never believed on its own.

Measure with sighting rather than drawing what you know the proportion is. This is the exercise where the stage 1 sighting work pays off most obviously.
One-point: a room from imagination, furn:
Norling is the gentlest introduction there is and the whole book is about ninety pages. One-point first because it has one vanishing point and no excuses.

A room from imagination: back wall square to the viewer, every orthogonal running to one point on the horizon. Then put furniture in it — a table, a chair, a door standing open — because the furniture is where it gets hard. A door swinging open leaves the one-point system and needs a vanishing point of its own.

Put the horizon at standing eye height and mark it. Perspective errors are almost always errors about where the horizon is.
Two-point: a building, once with the hor:
The same building drawn twice, identical in every way except the horizon line — once from above it, once from well below.

Drawing it twice is the lesson. It makes the horizon a decision you make rather than a default, and low-horizon is the dramatic one that most beginners never try. Keep both vanishing points on the page for the first attempt and well off it for the second, so you feel what a wide station point does.

Norling again, or D'Amelio if you want the construction stated more rigorously.
Three-point: looking up at something tal:
The third point goes above or below, and verticals converge toward it. Looking UP, so it is above and your verticals narrow toward the top.

The common failure is overdoing it — a slight convergence reads as a tall building, a strong one reads as a fish-eye lens. Put the third point a long way off the page for anything that is meant to look natural.

Worth doing once properly and then knowing it exists. Most drawing is two-point; three-point is for when the shot is the point.
100 ellipses in perspective, minor axis:
A hundred, freehand, no guide. The rule that makes them right: the MINOR axis of the ellipse lies along the axis of the cylinder, always, and is perpendicular to the major axis.

Most wrong ellipses are wrong because the minor axis is tilted off the cylinder's axis — a wheel that looks like it is falling off the car, a cup whose rim does not sit on the cup. Draw the axis line first, every time, then the ellipse around it.

Vary the degree: near-circle through to a sliver. Draw them in one confident motion rather than sketching round — ellipses are the clearest case where a fast line is more accurate than a careful one.
Place a figure correctly in a one-point:
The one piece of perspective that matters most for drawing people in places, and it is simple: on flat ground, the horizon crosses every standing figure of the same height at the same point on their body.

If the horizon is at your eye level, it crosses every standing adult at their eyes, near or far. So to place a figure, draw the horizon, decide where their feet land, and scale them so the horizon hits the same place on them as on the others.

This is also the test for whether a drawn scene is coherent. Figures that look wrong in an otherwise-good drawing are almost always failing this one rule.
Cast shadows from a single source in a c:
Shadows have their own perspective. A cast shadow is constructed from two points: the light source, and the point directly below it on the ground plane.

D'Amelio gives the construction properly — ray from the light over the top of the object, ray from the ground point through the object's base, and the shadow ends where they meet. Sunlight is the special case where the source is effectively infinite, so the rays are parallel.

Construct a few, then stop constructing and start estimating. The value of the construction is that it calibrates the estimate, not that you will ever do it on a finished drawing.
A street in two-point, from imagination:
Everything from stage 4 in one drawing: a street receding, buildings on both sides at an angle, a horizon you chose, figures scaled to it, and shadows from one consistent sun.

From imagination, which is the whole point — reference would do the perspective for you. Expect it to take several attempts and expect the first to come apart somewhere in the middle distance.

Keep the construction lines. A drawing with its scaffolding visible is more useful to look back at than a clean one.
One Shepherds location drawn in perspect:
The transfer. Take a place from the Shepherds map data — the Highfold, the wall, the power station — and draw it as a perspective view from inside it rather than the three-quarter top-down the game uses.

The game's camera flattens a lot of decisions. Drawing a location in proper perspective is how you find out whether the ground plan actually makes sense as a place: whether the yards are the right size, whether the gate is where a person walking would expect it, whether the buildings are too close.

This is a genuinely useful piece of production work and not just an exercise, which is why it closes the stage.
Draw the skeleton from memory, front and:
From memory, which means studying it until you can, not tracing it once.

You do not need every bone. You need the ones that show: skull, jaw, clavicles, ribcage shape and where it ends, spine curves, pelvis, the great trochanter, knee, ankle, and the two-bone arm and leg. Those are the landmarks every surface form sits on.

Goldfinger for accuracy, Simblet for how it looks on a living body — she photographs models beside the anatomy, which is the connection the older books leave you to make yourself.
Ribcage and pelvis as simple forms, 30 t:
The two masses, drawn as the simple solids they are, rotated through thirty orientations relative to each other.

This is the exercise that makes anatomy usable. Everything about a torso's shape comes from how these two boxes are tilted and twisted against one another — and that relationship is the whole of what a pose is above the legs.

Thirty, and vary BOTH: tilt, twist and side-bend. If the ribcage and pelvis stay parallel in all thirty you have drawn one pose thirty times.
The torso: constructive anatomy, front,:
Bridgman does not draw anatomy, he draws the wedges and blocks that anatomy makes, which is why he is still the one worth learning from.

The torso as he sees it: the chest wedge, the abdominal wedge, the pelvic wedge, and the way they interlock and shift. The back as a set of overlapping masses rather than a list of muscles.

His drawings are hard to read at first and that is not you. Copy them rather than looking at them — Bridgman is a book you draw through, not one you read.
Arms: the two-bone structure and what ro:
The forearm is two bones and one crosses over the other. That single fact explains almost every arm that looks wrong.

Palm up, radius and ulna are parallel. Palm down, the radius crosses over — which twists the whole mass of the forearm and changes its silhouette completely. Draw the same arm in both and watch the shape change.

The upper arm is simpler: one bone, and the deltoid capping the shoulder like a hood. Get the deltoid's insertion point right — it goes a third of the way down the upper arm, not at the shoulder.
Legs: the same, with weight on one side:
Two bones below the knee as well, but they do not rotate — the leg's complexity is in the thigh mass and the way the whole limb reads as two tapering forms that oppose each other.

The thing to get is the ZIGZAG: from the front, the thigh mass sits outboard, the calf mass inboard, and the ankle narrow, which is why a straight leg still reads as a curve. Hogarth and Bridgman both state it as explicit opposing rhythm.

With weight on one side, always. A leg bearing weight is a different shape from one that is not, and drawing both legs relaxed is how figures end up looking like they are hanging from a hook.
50 hands from life — your own is always:
Fifty, from life, your own non-drawing hand in a mirror or on the table.

Loomis' approach is to block the hand as a box for the palm with a separate wedge for the thumb, and only then find the fingers. Drawn finger-first the hand always comes out as five sausages, which is exactly what the stage 1 self-portrait will have shown you.

Two things to watch: the fingers do not start where they appear to — the knuckles of the hand are much further back than the webbing — and the fingers arc as a group rather than splaying independently. Hands are second only to heads in how hard a viewer judges them.
20 feet, which are harder than they look:
Twenty, because everyone skips feet and it shows.

A foot is a wedge with an arch, and the whole thing rests on three points — heel, ball of the big toe, outer edge. Drawn as a flat flipper it kills the figure's contact with the ground, which is the one thing a standing figure cannot afford to lose.

Draw them in shoes as well as bare. Shepherds' characters all wear boots, and a boot is a foot shape with its own construction on top rather than a blob.
Muscles of the back, named and drawn (Ho:
The back is where anatomy becomes visibly worth it, because there is almost no fat over it and the forms read directly.

The ones that matter: trapezius as a kite from skull to mid-back, latissimus wrapping from the lower spine to under the arm, the scapulae sliding across the ribcage as the arms move, and the erector spinae columns either side of the spine.

SCAPULAE MOVE. That is the thing to come away with. They are not fixed landmarks; they rotate and slide, and drawing them in the same place regardless of arm position is the commonest back error.

Hogarth is dramatic to the point of exaggeration. Take the structural clarity and leave the bodybuilder proportions.
A figure from imagination with anatomy t:
The stage test. One figure, invented pose, no reference, with anatomy that still holds up when you come back to it the next day.

"Survives a second look" is the acceptance criterion and it is deliberately subjective. What it means in practice: no limb of impossible length, joints where joints go, the ribcage and pelvis in a relationship a body could hold, weight resolved onto something.

If it fails, the fix is almost never more anatomy. It is construction — go back to the mannequin figures and rebuild on them.
The Loomis ball-and-plane head, 30 angle:
The single most useful construction in drawing. A sphere for the cranium, slice the sides flat, drop the jaw off it, and the whole head is locatable at any angle.

Thirty angles from imagination: looking up, down, over the shoulder, tipped, three-quarter rear. The method's value is exactly that it works at angles you have no reference for.

The part to get right is the centre line and the brow line drawn as curves wrapping the sphere, because those two lines place every feature. Get them wrapping correctly and the features land; draw them flat and the face slides off the skull.
50 eyes, from life and reference:
The eye is a sphere with lids draped over it, and almost every drawn eye fails because it is drawn as a flat almond with a circle in it.

Fifty, and build each one as a ball first. The upper lid has thickness and casts a shadow onto the eyeball. The lids' high points are offset — the upper peaks toward the nose, the lower toward the ear — and that offset is most of what makes an eye look like an eye.

From life for half of them. Photographs lose the wet highlight and the lid thickness, which are the two things that make it read as alive.
50 noses:
A wedge with a ball on the end and two wings. Nothing else.

Fifty, from every angle, and from below especially — the nose seen from below is the angle that defeats people and it is the one that appears every time a character looks down at something.

The nose is where the plane change of the whole face concentrates: top plane, two sides, and the underside, which is the darkest small shape on a lit face. Draw the planes rather than the outline and the nose stops looking stuck on.
50 mouths:
Not two lines. The mouth sits on the cylinder of the teeth and jaw, so it wraps, and the line between the lips is the only hard edge — the lip borders themselves are soft.

Fifty, including some open, some smiling, some from the side. The upper lip is usually darker than the lower because it angles away from the light, and the lower lip catches it. That value relationship does more than any contour.

Watch the corners. They sit deeper than the rest of the mouth, and a smile that goes wrong is nearly always a smile drawn as a wide line instead of corners pulling back around the cylinder.
50 ears — the one everybody skips:
Fifty, because you will skip them otherwise and then every head you draw will have two question marks on the sides.

The ear is a C of the outer rim with a Y inside it. That is the whole structure and it takes ten minutes to learn, which is why skipping it is so unnecessary.

Placement matters more than the shape: the ear sits between the brow line and the base of the nose, behind the vertical halfway line of the head, and it tilts back roughly parallel to the jaw. Get the placement right and a crudely drawn ear passes; get it wrong and a beautifully drawn one looks like an error.
Head proportions measured from life, not:
Measure a real head with sighting, write the numbers down, and compare them against what you have been assuming.

The ones people get wrong, consistently: the eyes are halfway down the head, not a third; the skull is much deeper front-to-back than it is wide; the ear is larger than expected; and the cranium above the brow is a bigger share of the whole than any symbol drawing allows.

Loomis' canon is a starting point, not a person. The point of measuring from life is to find where a specific head departs from the canon, because that departure is the likeness.
A portrait from life across three sittin:
One sitter, three sessions, the same drawing carried through.

Three sittings is the traditional structure for a reason: the first gets the construction and proportions, the second the form and value, the third the likeness and the finish. Trying to do all three in one session is how you end up with a careful drawing of nobody in particular.

From life, which means dealing with a head that moves, light that changes and a person who gets bored. All three are part of it. Mark the sitter's position and your own on the floor so the setup can be restored.
A portrait from a photograph, and the di:
The same effort from a photograph, then write down what was different. Not which was better — what was different.

What you will find: the photograph is easier because it has already flattened the form and fixed the light, and harder because it has thrown away the information you needed. Lens distortion lengthens whatever is nearest. Contrast is crushed in the shadows, so the reflected light that describes the form is simply not there.

This matters because almost all the reference you will use for Shepherds is photographic, and knowing what a photograph lies about is how you draw from one without inheriting its lies.
20 expressions from imagination (Hogarth:
Twenty, invented, no reference. Expression is muscle, and the muscles that make it are few: the brow group, the ring around the eye, the ring around the mouth, and the ones pulling the mouth corners.

Hogarth's treatment is systematic — he takes each expression down to which muscles contract and what that does to the surrounding forms. Use the system rather than copying his drawings, because his faces are very much his.

The test of a drawn expression is covering the mouth. If the eyes and brow alone still say what the face is feeling, it is real; if not, you have drawn a mouth shape.
One Shepherds character drawn as a portr:
Take a hero from the game and draw them as a head-and-shoulders portrait at full size, working from the 64 px sprite and whatever canon says about them.

This is a genuine production exercise. A sprite at that size carries maybe four decisions about a face, and a portrait forces every one of the others — what the jaw does, how old they actually are, what their expression rests at. Several of those answers are things canon has not written down, and finding out which is useful by itself.

Timon has final say on design, so this is a proposal rather than a decision. Draw it as one.
20 notan studies — two values only, no d:
Two values. Black and white, no grey, no line, no detail. Dow's term for the Japanese idea that a composition either works as a pattern of dark and light or does not work at all.

Twenty, each from a different source — a photograph, a film still, a painting, one of your own drawings. Small, a few inches across, and fast. Brush and ink or a marker, so greys are not available even if you want them.

The ones that still read at two values are compositions. The ones that turn to mud were relying on detail, and detail cannot save a composition that has no structure underneath it.
20 thumbnail compositions for a single s:
One subject, twenty different arrangements of it, each no bigger than a matchbox, then choose.

Twenty is the number that forces you past the obvious. The first three are what you already had in mind, the next ten are variations, and the useful ones are usually in the teens — after you have exhausted the comfortable options and have to try something you would not have chosen.

The choosing is part of the exercise. Pick one, write one sentence saying why, and build the stage's later work on it.
A nine-step value scale, drawn by hand a:
Nine steps from white to black, by hand, with even intervals. Harder than it sounds and worth the irritation.

The test is squinting at it: the steps should look evenly spaced with no jump and no pair that merges. Almost everyone's first attempt crowds the darks and spreads the lights, because pencil resists going genuinely black.

The reason to do it: you cannot control a value you cannot produce on demand. Everything in the rendering lessons assumes you can hit a stated value deliberately rather than by feel.
One drawing in five values, no more (Gup:
Five values, counted. Lightest light, light, mid, dark, darkest dark, and nothing between them.

The restriction is the lesson. With five values available you must decide what each one is FOR — which planes are lit, where the form turns, what is in shadow — rather than smoothly blending your way around the decision.

Guptill's Sketching and Rendering in Pencil is the technical reference here: how to get a flat even tone, how to vary edge quality, how to keep pencil work from going grey and dead. This also connects straight back to the Aseprite curriculum's three-or-four-values-per-material rule, which is the same discipline with a smaller budget.
Rendering: one subject taken to a finish:
One drawing taken all the way past where you want to stop.

Finish is a specific skill and it is not detail. It is edge control — hard edges where planes meet sharply, soft where they turn gradually, lost edges where a form disappears into a shadow of the same value. Lost edges are the ones that make a rendered drawing look like air rather than like a cutout.

Expect it to take several hours and expect to pass through a stage where it looks worse than it did an hour ago. That stage is normal and stopping there is why most studies stay studies.
Picture-making: the composition chapters:
Loomis on how a picture is organised: the arrangement of masses, the handling of the eye's path through it, and the difference between a drawing of something and a picture about something.

The chapters to work rather than read are the ones on informal subdivision and on the standard compositional patterns. Both are procedures — ways of arriving at an arrangement that is not symmetrical and not accidental.

This is the book that connects every earlier stage. By here you can draw a figure, put it in a space, light it and render it; what Loomis adds is why it should be arranged this way rather than that.
Colour: the first exercises in Edwards’:
Edwards' Color, the first exercises, and the honest framing: this is a colour-THEORY course rather than a book about light.

What it gives you properly is the vocabulary and the colour wheel exercises — hue, value, intensity as three independent dials, and the discipline of mixing a stated colour rather than approximating it. That is real and it is enough to start.

What it does not give you is how light behaves — bounce, ambient, colour temperature shifting across a form. Gurney's Color and Light is the standard for that and is not on the shelf; this is the point at which buying it would actually be justified.
One finished illustration of a Shepherds:
Everything, in one picture. A scene from the game — a moment from the Prologue, the wall at dawn, York from the ring road — composed from thumbnails, constructed in perspective, populated with figures that stand on the ground, lit from one source, rendered to a finish.

This is the exit exam for stages 1 to 7 and it should take days rather than hours. Choose a moment that already exists in the game so the subject is given and all the decisions left are drawing decisions.

It is also the first thing in this curriculum that is a deliverable rather than an exercise. Show it to Timon.
A sketchbook page a day, every day:
A page a day, no standard, no theme, no requirement that it be good.

The only rule that matters is that it is daily rather than long. Twenty minutes every day beats four hours on Sunday by a wide margin, because drawing is a motor skill and motor skills consolidate between sessions rather than during them.

Date every page. The sketchbook is the actual record of this curriculum — the milestones say what was studied, the sketchbook shows what it did.
10 figures a day from life or reference:
Ten a day, on top of the sketchbook page, forever.

This is maintenance rather than progress. Gesture decays faster than anything else in drawing: a fortnight off and the line goes tentative, a month off and you are back to outlining. Ten a day holds it.

They do not need to be good and they do not need to be kept. Five minutes with a timer and reference that changes on its own, before the real work of the day.
One finished piece a month, taken past t:
Twelve finished pieces a year, and "finished" is doing the work in that sentence.

The point where a drawing stops being fun is roughly the point where the discovery is over and only the execution is left — and everything that separates a study from a picture happens after it. Studies are comfortable and infinite; finishing is the uncomfortable part that actually improves the work.

One a month is a sustainable rate that still produces a body of work. Keep them together and in order.
Redraw the stage 1 pre-instruction drawi:
The self-portrait, your own hand, the chair. Same subjects, same time limit, no reference to the originals while drawing.

Then put them side by side. This is the only measurement in the curriculum that is not a count, and it is the one that answers the question the counts cannot: did any of it work?

"Honestly" means looking for what has NOT improved as hard as for what has. Something will have lagged — it is usually either hands or the ability to see your own proportion errors — and that is the next thing to work on rather than a reason to be disappointed.
Draw something for Shepherds every week:
One drawing a week that the game could use: a prop, a building, a character study, a piece of UI, a location in perspective.

The reason this is a standing milestone rather than a project is that the curriculum's whole justification is being able to contribute to and judge the game's art. A year of excellent studies that never touched Shepherds would have missed the point.

Timon has final say on design and draws by hand. These are proposals and references for him, not replacements — and the fastest way to become useful to someone who draws is to draw beside them.
Draw something purely because you wanted:
One drawing a week with no purpose. Not for the game, not for a milestone, not to practise anything.

This is in the curriculum deliberately. A structured path with counts and acceptance criteria is very good at producing competence and quite good at killing the reason you started, and the people who stop drawing mostly stop because every drawing had become homework.

No standard applies to these and they do not need to be shown to anybody.
